values.label: The grammar a town is generated by
values.reason: Authored: a town is generated by the city grammar, the one grammar whose records state streets, premises and the walking surfaces a society walks and traffic drives.

values.label: The version of that grammar
values.reason: Measured: version 5 lays the street mix and the use mix this schema offers, sets each stop line back from the crossing it approaches and keeps a parking lane against each kerb of a high street, which traffic derives its bays from, and dresses every surface a town draws. Measured over every point of this schema's lengths, storeys, high streets and cross streets, each number on its step and each choice taken, two towns at each with every share even, and at 24 of those points, the extremes of each, one town with each share alone at its most and one with every share at none: every town was made, its roads compiled for traffic, and every tile baked with every surface it draws dressed.

values.label: Length of the town, west to east
values.reason: Measured: whole 128 m tiles, two or three, because the terrain stage covers a town with whole tiles. One tile mostly does not generate (a kerb run too short for a crossing and the stop line before it), and four tiles held more people than a town's society ground admits. Three tiles need long blocks (the distance between cross streets says why), and with them the largest town this schema admits keeps its society's tick inside the tick budget the specification's bounds state.

values.label: Depth of the town, south to north
values.reason: Measured: one tile deep. A town two tiles deep lays junctions where two local streets both run on through, and traffic refuses a junction whose every approach has priority: 23 of 23 such towns had their traffic refused, 14 for that reason.

values.label: Distance between cross streets

requires.reason: Measured: a town three tiles long needs cross streets at least 130 m apart. With 90 to 120 m most of its seed candidates held more people than its society ground admits or did not generate at all (with 120 m none of 10), and the towns that were kept held as many people as the ground admits on walking graphs of 1,100 to 1,180 places, where one tick took 154 ms at the median and 197 ms at the 95th percentile, at the edge of the tick budget; with 130 and 140 m, 24 of 24 towns tried were kept, on graphs of at most 906 places.

values.reason: Measured: 90 to 140 m in 10 m steps. A town two tiles long takes every length offered: the kerb of the town's edge that runs straight on past a tile's 64 m margin is drawn without the kerb it runs on into, which the tessellator drew only with it when version 1 of this schema was measured and so held two-tile towns to 120 m. Three-tile towns need 130 or 140 m, the requirement says why. Shorter blocks leave kerb runs too short for a crossing and a stop line; longer ones leave a two-tile town one block wide. Measured over every point of this schema's lengths, storeys, high streets and cross streets, each number on its step and each choice taken, two towns at each with every share even, and at 24 of those points, the extremes of each, one town with each share alone at its most and one with every share at none: every town was made, its roads compiled for traffic, and every tile baked with every surface it draws dressed.

values.label: Depth of a block
values.reason: Measured: 56 m. With 60 m blocks no town one tile deep generated (0 of 120), because no street fits behind the high street; with 52 m blocks traffic compiled for 39 of 60 two-tile towns and with 56 m for 56 of 60; with 48 m a crossing often falls inside two junctions.

values.label: Fewest storeys a building has
values.reason: Measured: two or three storeys, the low end of a town's street wall. Bands of 2 to 4 and 3 to 5 storeys both generated every two-tile town tried; a band below its fewest is never offered, since the most storeys start at four.

values.label: Most storeys a building has
values.reason: Measured: four or five storeys, a small town rather than a corridor of six-storey walls. Taller buildings hold more homes, and five storeys kept every two-tile town tried within the people one tick of its society was measured to hold.

values.label: How many high streets
values.reason: Measured: the street through the town's middle is a high street, and each further one is a cross street, the nearest the middle first, so a second high street crosses the first where the street along the town keeps priority. Every town this schema offers lays two cross streets, so it holds one to three high streets; a town one tile deep has no room for a second high street along its length. A high street's ground floors are shops and its kerbs keep parking. Measured over every point of this schema's lengths, storeys, high streets and cross streets, each number on its step and each choice taken, two towns at each with every share even, and at 24 of those points, the extremes of each, one town with each share alone at its most and one with every share at none: every town was made, its roads compiled for traffic, and every tile baked with every surface it draws dressed.

values.label: The other cross streets
values.reason: Measured: a cross street that is not a high street is a local street, or a narrow street with a narrower footway, a lower kerb and slower traffic; both carry traffic both ways. values.label: The side of the road traffic keeps to
values.reason: Authored: the right, because the traffic simulation drives on the right only (docs/traffic-contract.md, its limits), and the grammar requires the side to be stated.

values.label: Rise and fall of the ground
values.reason: Authored: level ground, because the terrain stage generates level ground only and walking surfaces stay within the step the city grammar publishes.

values.label: Width of a gutter
values.reason: Authored: 300 mm, one width for the whole town, because the streets stage reads one gutter width along a whole street and refuses to derive it block by block.

values.label: Radius of a street corner's kerb
values.reason: Measured: 4 m at every corner, one radius for the whole town. With radii drawn per block from 1.5 to 15 m, traffic refused the roads of 6 of 48 towns probed below this gate (a connection whose corner no vehicle can turn, or a space reached inside a junction's zone), and the first 98 towns of this schema's sweep before this value held 8 refused and 3 whose cross streets ran shorter than a car needs between a high street and the town's edge, so they had no vehicle; with 4 m, 72 of 72 towns probed (two and three tiles, one to three high streets, local and narrow cross streets) drove every trip. Small radii for slow urban turns are discussed in NACTO Urban Street Design Guide (Island Press, 2013), Street Design Elements, Corner Radii, which was not re-read in this build and is not quoted.

values.label: How far buildings stand back from the footway
values.reason: Authored: none, so buildings stand on their frontage line and make the unbroken street edge of a town centre, as the small town and the corridor do.

values.label: Lots kept back as memory precincts
values.reason: Authored: none, so every lot is built on and every building can hold homes and shops.

tick.reason: Measured with scripts/measure_generated_world.py inside the machine-wide quiet slot, over 8 market towns three tiles long with cross streets 140 m apart, two to four storeys, one high street, local cross streets and every share even, the values whose towns held the most places over this schema's sweep (walking graphs of up to 962 nodes in those towns): one purposeful tick of the most people its society ground admits, 128, took 130 ms at the median and 159 ms at the 95th percentile on the largest graph, and the most people any of those towns held, 90, took 90 and 131 ms.

refusals.meaning: The schema states no adjustable value with this key: it is not a value a world states, or the schema fixes it (its reason says why).
The value is outside the range the schema states for its key, off its step, or not the kind of value the key takes; the refusal names the key, the value and the range.

Two values the schema does not admit together: while one lies in a stated range, the other's range narrows (its ``requires`` says when and why). The refusal names both keys, both values and the narrowed range.
No seed candidate made a world from these values: the grammar refused each, or its homes housed nobody. Every candidate's refusal is named.
